title: Infinite Series
lead: An infinite series adds infinitely many terms, and its value is the limit of its partial sums, a sequence of finite sums. The harmonic series and the geometric series are the first series met, and telescoping series are those whose partial sums collapse to a first and a last term.
objectives: Explain the meaning of the sum of an infinite series.
Calculate the sum of a geometric series.
summary_html:
• Given the infinite series $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\kaseq_{n}=\kaseq_{1}+\kaseq_{2}+\kaseq_{3}+\cdots$$ and the corresponding sequence of partial sums $\{\kS_{k}\}$ where $$\kS_{k}=\sum_{n=1}^{k}\kaseq_{n}=\kaseq_{1}+\kaseq_{2}+\kaseq_{3}+\cdots+\kaseq_{k},$$ the series converges if and only if the sequence $\{\kS_{k}\}$ converges.
  • The geometric series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}ar^{n-1}$ converges if $|r|\lt 1$ and diverges if $|r|\ge1.$ For $|r|\lt 1,$ $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}ar^{n-1}=\frac{a}{1-r}.$$
  • The harmonic series $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}=1+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\cdots$$ diverges.
  • A series of the form $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} [\kbseq_{n}-\kbseq_{n+1}]=[\kbseq_{1}-\kbseq_{2}]+[\kbseq_{2}-\kbseq_{3}]+[\kbseq_{3}-\kbseq_{4}]+\cdots+[\kbseq_{n}-\kbseq_{n+1}]+\cdots$ is a telescoping series. The $k\text{th}$ partial sum of this series is given by $\kS_{k}=\kbseq_{1}-\kbseq_{k+1}.$ The series will converge if and only if $\lim_{k\to \infty}\kbseq_{k+1}$ exists. In that case, $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} [\kbseq_{n}-\kbseq_{n+1}]=\kbseq_{1}-\lim_{k\to \infty}(\kbseq_{k+1}).$$

exercises.prompt: Determine whether the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(n+1)/n$ converges or diverges.

answer.solution: The series diverges because the $k\text{th}$ partial sum $\kS_{k}\gt k.$
answer.hint: Look at the sequence of partial sums.

In the following exercises, compute the general term $\kaseq_{n}$ of the series with the given partial sum $\kS_{n}.$ If the sequence of partial sums converges, find its limit $\kSsum.$

$\kS_{n}=\sqrt{n},n\ge2$

answer.solution: $\kaseq_{n}=\kS_{n}-\kS_{n-1}=\sqrt{n}-\sqrt{n-1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n-1}+\sqrt{n}}.$ Series diverges because partial sums are unbounded.

exercises.prompt:

Suppose that $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \kaseq_{n}=1,$ that $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \kbseq_{n}=-1,$ that $\kaseq_{1}=2,$ and $\kbseq_{1}=-3.$ Find the sum of the indicated series.

State whether the given series converges and explain why.

$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n+1000}$ (Hint: Rewrite using a change of index.)

State whether the given series converges and explain why.

$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n+{10}^{80}}$ (Hint: Rewrite using a change of index.)

answer.solution: Diverges. With the change of index $m=n+10^{80},$ the series is $\sum_{m=10^{80}+1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{m},$ the harmonic series with its first $10^{80}$ terms left out. Leaving out finitely many terms does not change whether a series converges, and the harmonic series diverges, so this series diverges too.

exercises.prompt:
State whether the given series converges and explain why.

$1+\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{100}+\frac{1}{1000}+\cdots$

State whether the given series converges and explain why.

$1+\frac{e}{\pi}+\frac{e^{2}}{\pi^{2}}+\frac{e^{3}}{\pi^{3}}+\cdots$

answer.solution: Converges. This is a geometric series with initial term $a=1$ and ratio $r=\frac{e}{\pi}\approx 0.865.$ Since $|r|\lt 1,$ it converges, to $\frac{1}{1-e/\pi}=\frac{\pi}{\pi-e}.$

exercises.prompt:
State whether the given series converges and explain why.

$1+\frac{\pi}{e^{2}}+\frac{\pi^{2}}{e^{4}}+\frac{\pi^{3}}{e^{6}}+\frac{\pi^{4}}{e^{8}}+\cdots$

State whether the given series converges and explain why.

$1-\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{3}}+\sqrt{\frac{\pi^{2}}{9}}-\sqrt{\frac{\pi^{3}}{27}}+\cdots$

answer.solution: Diverges. Since $\sqrt{\frac{\pi^{k}}{3^{k}}}=(\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{3}})^{k},$ this is the geometric series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{3}})^{n-1}$ with ratio $r=-\sqrt{\pi/3}.$ Since $\pi\gt 3,$ $|r|=\sqrt{\pi/3}\approx 1.023\gt 1,$ so the series diverges.

[T] A fair coin is one that has probability $1/2$ of coming up heads when flipped.

  1. What is the probability that a fair coin will come up tails $n$ times in a row?
  2. Find the probability that a coin comes up heads for the first time on the last of an even number of coin flips.

answer.solution: 1. The probability of any given ordered sequence of outcomes for $n$ coin flips is $1/2^{n}.$ b. The probability of coming up heads for the first time on the $n$ th flip is the probability of the sequence $TT\ldots TH$ which is $1/2^{n}.$ The probability of coming up heads for the first time on an even flip is $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 1/2^{2n}$ or $1/3.$

exercises.prompt: [T] Find the probability that a fair coin will come up heads for the second time after an even number of flips.

[T] The expected number of times that a fair coin will come up heads is defined as the sum over $n=1,2\text{,\ldots}$ of $n$ times the probability that the coin will come up heads exactly $n$ times in a row, or $n/2^{n+1}.$ Compute the expected number of consecutive times that a fair coin will come up heads.

answer.solution: $E=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n/2^{n+1}=1,$ as can be shown using summation by parts

exercises.prompt: [T] Suppose that the amount of a drug in a patient’s system diminishes by a multiplicative factor $r\lt 1$ each hour. Suppose that a new dose is administered every $N$ hours. Find an expression that gives the amount $A(n)$ in the patient’s system after $n$ hours for each $n$ in terms of the dosage $d$ and the ratio $r.$ (Hint: Write $n=mN+k,$ where $0\le k\lt N,$ and sum over values from the different doses administered.)

answer.solution:
The part of the first dose after $n$ hours is $dr^{n},$ the part of the second dose is $dr^{n-N},$ and, in general, the part remaining of the $m\text{th}$ dose is $dr^{n-mN},$ so

$A(n)=\sum_{l=0}^{m} dr^{n-lN}=\sum_{l=0}^{m} dr^{k+(m-l)N}=\sum_{q=0}^{m} dr^{k+qN}=dr^{k}\sum_{q=0}^{m} r^{Nq}=dr^{k}\frac{1-r^{(m+1)N}}{1-r^{N}},n=k+mN.$

exercises.prompt: Suppose that $\kaseq_{n}\ge0$ is a sequence of numbers. Explain why the sequence of partial sums of $\kaseq_{n}$ is increasing.

[T] Suppose that $\kaseq_{n}$ is a sequence of positive numbers and the sequence $\kS_{n}$ of partial sums of $\kaseq_{n}$ is bounded above. Explain why $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \kaseq_{n}$ converges. Does the conclusion remain true if we remove the hypothesis $\kaseq_{n}\ge0\text{?}$

answer.solution: Since every $a_{n}\gt 0,$ $S_{n+1}=S_{n}+a_{n+1}\gt S_{n},$ so the sequence of partial sums is increasing. It is bounded above by hypothesis, so by the Monotone Convergence Theorem it converges, and therefore the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_{n}$ converges. The conclusion fails without $a_{n}\ge 0:$ for $a_{n}={(-1)}^{n},$ the partial sums $-1,0,-1,0,\ldots$ are bounded above by $0,$ but they do not converge, and the series diverges.

exercises.prompt: [T] Suppose that $\kaseq_{1}=\kS_{1}=1$ and that, for given numbers $\kSsum\gt 1$ and $0\lt k\lt 1,$ one defines $\kaseq_{n+1}=k(\kSsum-\kS_{n})$ and $\kS_{n+1}=\kaseq_{n+1}+\kS_{n}.$ Does $\kS_{n}$ converge? If so, to what? (Hint: First argue that $\kS_{n}\lt \kSsum$ for all $n$ and $\kS_{n}$ is increasing.)

answer.solution: Since $\kSsum\gt 1,$ $\kaseq_{2}\gt 0,$ and since $k\lt 1,$ $\kS_{2}=1+\kaseq_{2}\lt 1+(\kSsum-1)=\kSsum.$ If $\kS_{n}\gt \kSsum$ for some n, then there is a smallest n. For this n, $\kSsum\gt \kS_{n-1},$ so $\kS_{n}=\kS_{n-1}+k(\kSsum-\kS_{n-1})$ $=kS+(1-k)\kS_{n-1}\lt \kSsum,$ a contradiction. Thus $\kS_{n}\lt \kSsum$ and $\kaseq_{n+1}\gt 0$ for all n, so $\kS_{n}$ is increasing and bounded by $\kSsum.$ Let $\kS_{\text{∗}}=\lim \kS_{n}.$ If $\kS_{\text{∗}}\lt \kSsum,$ then $\delta =k(\kSsum-\kS_{\text{∗}})\gt 0,$ but we can find n such that $\kS_{*}-\kS_{n}\lt \delta /2,$ which implies that $\kS_{n+1}=\kS_{n}+k(\kSsum-\kS_{n})$ $\gt \kS_{*}+\delta /2,$ contradicting that $\kS_{n}$ is increasing to $\kS_{\text{∗}}.$ Thus $\kS_{n}\to \kSsum.$

exercises.prompt: [T] Suppose that $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \kaseq_{n}$ is a convergent series of positive terms. Explain why $\lim_{N\to \infty}\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} \kaseq_{n}=0.$

answer.solution: Let $\kS_{k}=\sum_{n=1}^{k} \kaseq_{n}$ and $\kS_{k}\to L.$ Then $\kS_{k}$ eventually becomes arbitrarily close to $L,$ which means that $L-\kS_{N}=\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} \kaseq_{n}$ becomes arbitrarily small as $N\to \infty.$

exercises.prompt: [T] The Sierpinski gasket is obtained by dividing the unit square into nine equal sub-squares, removing the middle square, then doing the same at each stage to the remaining sub-squares. The figure shows the remaining set after four iterations. Compute the total area removed after $N$ stages, and compute the length the total perimeter of the remaining set after $N$ stages.

answer.solution:
At stage one a square of area $1/9$ is removed, at stage $2$ one removes $8$ squares of area $1/9^{2},$ at stage three one removes $8^{2}$ squares of area $1/9^{3},$ and so on. The total removed area after $N$ stages is $\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} 8^{N}/9^{N+1}=\frac{1}{8}(1-{(8/9)}^{N})/(1-8/9)\to 1$

as $N\to \infty.$ The total perimeter is $4+4\underset{n=0}{\sum}8^{N}/3^{N+1}\to \infty.$

Each term of a group is at least the group's last term: $\frac{1}{3}\gt\frac{1}{4},$ and $\frac{1}{5},\frac{1}{6},\frac{1}{7}$ are each more than $\frac{1}{8}.$
The group ending at $\frac{1}{2^{i}}$ has $2^{i-1}$ terms, each at least $\frac{1}{2^{i}};$ for $j\gt 1$ the group $\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{4}$ is strictly larger than $2(\frac{1}{4}).$
There are $j$ halves, one for $\frac{1}{2}$ and one for each of the $j-1$ groups.
